title: Too Much Feedback, Too Little Modelling
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele argues that post-observation feedback in schools routinely violates the cognitive-load principles those same schools ask teachers to apply to students. He opens with the familiar post-observation gap: a lesson that felt successful in the room comes back as a list of missed strategies — you didn't check on your PP students, didn't teach key vocabulary, didn't use that retrieval strategy. His first objection is evidential: those things often did happen, just outside the observed window, or were rightly not attempted because the moment or the class did not suit them. The second objection is the irony at the centre of the piece — leadership teams who warn against overloading students issue feedback that is dense, checklist-heavy and stuffed with next steps, none of which land. The remedy he proposes is live modelling during feedback, citing Steplab's documentary The Great Teaching Unpacked, where teachers and leaders role-play a feedback move together rather than merely naming it, turning evaluation into coaching. His operational rule is one actionable focus rather than eight fixes, on the grounds that anything more dilutes impact. He closes by conceding that most school leaders mean well, and asking whether they are doing for teachers what they expect teachers to do for students.
points: The load argument is the piece's spine: feedback that is dense and checklist-driven fails for the same reason an overloaded explanation fails, which makes it a professional-development design problem rather than a tone problem.
Emanuele challenges the evidentiary basis of snapshot feedback — a strategy's absence from a twenty-minute window is not evidence of its absence from the teacher's practice.
He defends the legitimacy of not using a strategy: not every lesson suits Turn and Talk, and some classes are not ready, so an unticked box can reflect good judgement.
Role-played, live-modelled feedback is offered as the concrete alternative — showing the move in a group rehearsal rather than naming it, which converts feedback from evaluative to developmental.
The one-focus rule gives leaders an implementable constraint: a single embeddable action per observation, with more treated as a cost rather than as generosity.
quotes: Every teacher knows that post-observation feeling. You’ve just finished a solid lesson: students were engaged, they made progress, behaviour was calm, yet the feedback form doesn’t quite reflect the success you felt in the room.

But here’s the issue: sometimes those things did happen but just not in that small window of the lesson that was observed. Or maybe, quite simply, it wasn’t the right moment for that particular strategy.

Teachers are told to make our instructions to students clear, concise, and free from cognitive overload. However, the feedback they receive can be the complete opposite: dense, checklist-heavy, and packed with so many “next steps” that none of them truly land.

They don’t just say “you could try narrating behaviour” — they act it out, together, in groups. This approach transforms feedback from something abstract and evaluative into something collaborative and developmental. It’s feedback as coaching, not criticism.
The best feedback isn’t a list of eight things to fix; it’s one actionable focus that a teacher can actually embed. Anything more than that adds unnecessary cognitive load and dilutes the impact.
When feedback is simplified, focused, and modelled live, it becomes empowering rather than overwhelming. Teachers leave the room feeling supported, not judged.

There are many brilliant schools in England where leaders genuinely care about staff wellbeing and professional growth. But sometimes, in their eagerness to help teachers improve, they accidentally create the very thing they warn against: cognitive overload.
